title: This too trains
hook: how to bear a fever: this too is exercise (Discourses 3.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was unhindered, the will Epictetus hoped death would find calm and free. Your line was attending to nothing but my own will.
screen: `FOUND DOING THIS — ATTENDING TO NOTHING BUT MY OWN WILL.`

segments.voice: The thermometer beeps, and the week's plans quietly fall apart. Meetings get canceled, the to-do list sits there, and on top of feeling awful it's easy to feel useless, as if life is on pause until you're well. Epictetus knew something about bodies that don't cooperate. Ancient writers say he was lame. When he talks about illness, he isn't speaking from a healthy distance.
screen: `THE THERMOMETER BEEPS.` → `LIFE ON PAUSE.` → `ANCIENT WRITERS SAY HE WAS LAME.`

segments.voice: Discourses book three, chapter ten: how we should bear illness. It starts like a packing list. Keep your principles ready for each situation: at the table, the ones about eating; in the bath, the ones about bathing; in bed, the ones about lying in bed. And the ones about fever. A fever, he says, is part of life too, like walking, sailing or traveling. It isn't a pause. It's a different kind of practice. So what does bearing a fever well look like? He's specific. Not blaming God or other people. Not being crushed by what's happening. Doing what needs to be done. When the doctor comes in, not dreading what he'll say, and not giddy if he says you're doing well. The same things he asks on a healthy day, in a smaller room. This too is training, he says. A sick day isn't a day off from becoming who you want to be. In some ways it's a clear day for it, because the usual props are gone. You can't prove anything by being busy. You can only be patient, honest about how you feel, and kind to whoever brings the soup. This isn't a reason to ignore medicine or push through when your body needs rest. Resting well is the practice. The person lying there is still training, and still free.
screen: `PRINCIPLES READY FOR EVERY ROOM.` · `A FEVER IS PART OF LIFE TOO.` · `NOT BLAMING, NOT CRUSHED.` · `REST WELL: THAT'S THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `THIS TOO TRAINS.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whichever is kinder to your body right now, and scan gently from head to feet, noticing any ache, tiredness or tightness without fighting it or dramatizing it. Say plainly: this is here. Then ask how you'd like to carry it today: with patience, with honesty, or simply by resting well.
Nosos. Greek for sickness: Epictetus on illness, a fever is part of life, and bearing it well, without blame or despair, is practice like any other.
Your line: resting well is the practice. A fever is part of life, and so is bearing it well. Day four hundred nineteen, done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners who are ill treat recovery as part of their practice: following medical care, resting, and working on patience rather than blame.

sources.ref: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53; Simplicius, Commentary on the Enchiridion

notes: Discourses 3.10 paraphrased: principles ready at hand (dinner, bath, bed); fever as part of life; bearing fever well (not blaming God or man, not afflicted, the physician's visit); 'this too is a kind of exercise/test'. Confirm details.
Epictetus' lameness: Origen (Contra Celsum 7.53) reports the story of his master twisting his leg; Simplicius says he was lame from childhood; the Suda says from rheumatism. Confirm the summary.
The script adds that this isn't a reason to ignore medicine; check framing.
